transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-03-05
Start: 16:00 PST
Duration: ~47 minutes (recorded)
Attendees: Sofia Patel (Redwood AE), Ethan Ross (Redwood SE), Lena Ortega (QuantumGuard CTO), Marcus Hale (QuantumGuard ML Eng), Priya Singh (QuantumGuard Infra)

Auto-generated summary: (may be noisy) A technical review of prefix caching strategy, talking about hit rates, cache keys, tenant safety, adaptive TTLs, and pilot steps.

00:00 Sofia (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we wanted to walk through a very targeted review of QuantumGuard's prefix caching strategy — especially around noisy tenants and adaptive TTLs. I'm Sofia, AE. Ethan and I will lead the tech bits.
00:24 Ethan (SE): Hi all. Quick ask up front: Marcus, can you confirm the model families you're running in prod? You mentioned a mixture of 7B and 13B variants in the doc.
00:38 Marcus: Yeah, so the bulk is our 7B transformer for chat assistants, and a smaller set of customers hit the 13B for higher fidelity tasks. We also run some quantized 4-bit replicas for batch offline scoring.
01:05 Lena: And infra context — we run in a VPC peered to our cloud account, we can't do open internet model pulls so private deployment options matter to us.
01:13 Sofia: Got it. We'll flag the Private / VPC notes as we go. Okay, first slide — current cache behavior (Marcus sent a CSV): main points are very skewed prefix distribution, top 1% prefixes account for ~42% of requests, long tail is lots of single-shot prompts.
01:44 Marcus: Yep that matches our logs, though the CSV is sampled so numbers are a little rough.
01:50 Ethan: Cool. Two immediate levers: cache key design and TTLs/eviction policy. If keys are too coarse we get cross-tenant contamination; if too granular we miss hits.
02:10 Priya: We worry about a noisy tenant blowing out the shared cache and increasing p95 latency, and also cost. Do you have a recommended quarantine pattern?
02:23 Ethan: Yes — we typically recommend a tenant-aware scoring that tracks per-tenant hit rate, miss amplification, and token cost. When a tenant's miss amplification passes a threshold for N minutes, we shift them to a quarantined policy: smaller shared-key window, local-only cache, or bypass to dedicated routing.
02:46 Lena: By "miss amplification" do you mean the ratio of cache misses to total requests or something more nuanced?
02:52 Ethan: Good question — we define miss amplification as additional tokens executed server-side per request because the prefix wasn't cached times request rate, normalized by token cost. So it's more cost-aware.
03:15 Marcus: I like that. What threshold are we talking about? 10x over baseline?
03:20 Ethan: It's workload dependent. Our default pilot threshold is 5x sustained for 10 minutes, or a burst threshold of 20x for 30 seconds. Those numbers are configurable.
03:33 Sofia: We should also talk about cache key composition. Marcus, what fields do you include in your current prefix key?
03:40 Marcus: Right now it's basically model + prompt_family_id + immediate user prefix token hash. No tenant id in the key because we were hoping to get multi-tenant sharing benefits.
03:52 Ethan: That's the tradeoff. Without tenant id you get higher global hit rates but risk PII/tenant safety concerns and noisy tenant pathology. We propose a hybrid key: model + prompt_family + tenant_shard + prefix_hash where tenant_shard is a configurable bucketing (e.g. 256-way) to allow safe sharing while limiting cross-tenant leakage.
04:20 Lena: If we shard, do we lose some hit rate? Our top prefixes are shared across customers (generic system prompts).
04:28 Ethan: Some loss, yes. In the simulation we ran on a typical enterprise workload we saw a ~6-9% relative drop in global hit rate at 256-way sharding versus fully global, but tail latency improved for noisy tenant scenarios. The cost savings net still favored sharding because it prevents evictions caused by heavy tenants.
04:52 Marcus: Could we do selective global keys for known-safe system-level prompts and shard for user prompts?
05:00 Ethan: Absolutely. We support label-based key rules: whitelist of safe prompt_families that skip tenant_shard, everything else goes through tenant_shard. That gives a best-of-both worlds approach.
05:17 Priya: About adaptive TTLs — how quickly do TTLs adapt? If someone has a sudden campaign we don't want the cache to throw away good prefixes too fast.
05:27 Ethan: Our adaptive TTL controller looks at prefix reuse half-life. It keeps an exponential moving average of inter-arrival times per prefix (or per prefix bucket) and increases TTL for high-reuse prefixes and decays for low reuse. There are safety clamps — min TTL and max TTL; pilot defaults are min 30s, max 24h, but tunable.
05:51 Marcus: That sounds compute-heavy. How much state does that require? Our preference is low memory on the K V store.
05:58 Ethan: You can do it on a per-prefix-sample basis with reservoir sampling and maintain small footprints: e.g., store last_seen_ts and a count or decay scalar per prefix key. For high-cardinality tails we treat them differently — sample only top N prefixes, the rest use family-level heuristics.
06:24 Lena: Can you run that off Redis or do you need a custom K V tier?
06:29 Ethan: Both possible. Redis works for many customers with sharded clusters and TTL co-processors, but for very high QPS we push hot-key handling to the runtime memory (local cache) plus a distributed LRU. Redwood's runtime supports both levels and automatic prefix promotion.
06:49 Marcus: On quantization: we do 4-bit quantized versions for some models. Does quantization change cache semantics?
06:56 Ethan: Not for the cache keys; keys are model + prefix metadata — but quantization changes execution latency and batching tradeoffs. A quantized model might be cheaper per-token but less predictable at different sequence lengths. That impacts the decision threshold for quarantine because cost per miss changes.
07:23 Sophie — transcript misspell: Sofia: Sorry.
07:25 Ethan: Also be careful: cross-model key reuse can be allowed if models are architecturally compatible. We sometimes allow LLM variants (7B float vs 7B quant) to share keys when signature indicates same decoder behavior, but usually we separate keys across major architecture differences.
07:50 Marcus: How about prefetching / speculative warmups? We have recurring user flows where we can predict the next prompt family.
07:58 Ethan: Prefetching is effective for predictable flows. We recommend background prefetches with low priority and a soft limit to avoid displacing hot entries. Also mark prefetched keys with lower TTL until confirmed by real traffic.
08:26 Lena: Any security/regulatory concerns? We must ensure tenant data isn't leaked via shared cache hits or side channels.
08:34 Ethan: Right. For regulated data, we recommend per-tenant only caching, or use keyed encryption at rest + KMS-bound access logs. Also audit logs for cache promotions and evictions. For additional isolation you can push that tenant to Redwood Dedicated / Private where the cache is per-customer.
08:58 Sofia: Quick poll — would QuantumGuard prefer a per-tenant silo for sensitive customers and a shared pool for general customers?
09:05 Lena: That seems reasonable — we'll identify the top 5 regulated tenants for per-tenant siloing initially.
09:12 Priya: On metrics and SLOs: what do you recommend we measure for the pilot?
09:19 Ethan: Hit rate (global and per-tenant), miss amplification, p50/p95 token latency, cost per 1k tokens, and eviction churn. Also number of quarantine events and time in quarantine. We'll provide dashboards.
09:37 Marcus: Can you share the simulation notebook you mentioned earlier?
09:41 Sofia: Yes — I'll share the notebook and a cache-key checklist. Link in action items.
09:48 Ethan: For the VPC/on-prem pilot we need three things from you: sample prefix distribution, typical request QPS, and a list of high-sensitivity tenants. That will let us size the KV layer and set quarantine thresholds.
10:05 Marcus: We'll extract that and drop it in the secure folder.
10:10 Priya: About routing — you mentioned fallback to dedicated routing when quarantined; how transparent is that to the app?
10:18 Ethan: Transparent at the API layer; routing decisions happen server-side. The app gets the same API behaviour; we surface a header and audit log so you can see which requests were routed to dedicated capacity. For some customers we also expose a routing tag in logs.
10:36 Sofia: Let's pick concrete pilot success criteria: 1) 10% reduction in per-token cost for the shared workloads without increasing p95 by more than 10%, 2) quarantine reduces tail latency for noisy tenants by 30% within first two weeks, 3) accurate dashboarding for per-tenant hit rates.
11:02 Lena: Those look fine, subject to data once you run the sim.
11:10 Ethan: One noisy note — we saw in one customer case that overly aggressive prefetching actually reduced hit rate because of TTL churn. So our pilot will be conservative with prefetching enabled only for the top 20 families.
11:30 Marcus: Any gotchas around caching and function/tool calling? We use tool calls (external APIs) in prompts occasionally.
11:38 Ethan: Tool outputs must be treated carefully — unless you canonicalize tool output in the prefix, we recommend skipping caching for tool-augmented prefixes, or include a tool-output-hash in the key if you intend to cache.
11:55 Sofia: Great. Recap — action items and next steps as in the notes. We'll run a 2-week sim then a small VPC pilot with dedicated logging.
12:06 Lena: Thanks all. That was useful.
12:10 Meeting end.

References shared: "prefix-cache design doc" (https://redwood.ai/internal/prefix-cache), pilot config gist (https://redwood.ai/gists/qg-pilot-config), security checklist (https://redwood.ai/security/cache-isolation).
